section_summary: This section concludes a South Manchuria Railway Company financial statement for 1937–38, then presents detailed American consular reporting on the company’s 1939–40 budget and its balance sheet for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1939. The reports emphasize the railway’s profitable operations, expanding industrial and transport investments, growing debenture burden, and use by the Kwantung Army and Japanese government as an instrument of imperial policy in Manchuria and North China. The final documents concern locomotive parts stranded at Hong Kong and diplomatic efforts to determine whether the Japanese-controlled Peiping–Suiyuan Railway, the Bank of China, or the Chinese government should arrange their delivery.

subfiles.title: South Manchuria Railway Company balance sheet and profit accounts for the year ending March 31, 1938
subfiles.about: Financial tables state the company’s assets, liabilities, income, expenditure, profit, and disposition of profit for fiscal 1937–38.
subfiles.summary: The statement lists fixed assets, investments, current assets, unadjusted accounts, capital, reserves, bonds, deposits, and other liabilities totaling approximately ¥2.243 billion. The profit-and-loss account reports net profit of about ¥73.929 million. The disposition schedule provides for government and public dividends, reserves, officials’ bonuses, and a balance carried forward.

subfiles.title: Review of Dairen Despatch No. 99 on the South Manchuria Railway Company budget
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes the company’s exceptionally large 1939–40 budget and the strain caused by its imperial-policy obligations.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes total proposed expenditure of ¥408.908 million, including a ¥50 million supplementary budget. Much of the money was intended for new and double-tracked Manchukuo railway lines, strategic improvements, and investment in the North China Traffic Company. It concludes that the company’s financial problems arose from its simultaneous roles as a profitable business and an instrument of empire.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 99: Budget of the South Manchuria Railway Company for the Fiscal Year Ending March 31, 1940
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Turner analyzes the company’s 1939–40 enterprise budget, financing requirements, projected operating results, and strategic obligations.
subfiles.summary: The despatch reports an enterprise budget of ¥358.908 million plus a ¥50 million supplementary appropriation for transport capacity. It describes spending on railways, harbors, coal, shale oil, steel, and related companies, while emphasizing that expenditures on Manchukuo State Railways chiefly served Kwantung Army strategy. Turner discusses government capital payments, debenture financing, possible recapitalization, projected revenue and profit, and pressure from shareholders for higher dividends.

subfiles.title: Translation: Budget of the South Manchuria Railway Company for the Fiscal Year Ending March 31, 1940
subfiles.to: Public announcement; translated by the American Consulate at Dairen
subfiles.about: The enclosure supplies the company’s official budget announcement and comparative tables for 1938–39 and 1939–40.
subfiles.summary: The announcement divides projected enterprise expenditure among ordinary company enterprises, special company enterprises, and investments outside the company. It itemizes work at the Showa Steel Works, Dairen and Yingkou harbors, Fushun mines and oil plants, and Manchukuo railways. Comparative revenue and expenditure tables project revenue of ¥381.203 million and a surplus of ¥62.386 million.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 124: Balance Sheet of the South Manchuria Railway Company for the Fiscal Year Ended March 31, 1939
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Turner examines the company’s 1938–39 finances, business operations, investments, debt, profits, and dependence on Japanese military policy.
subfiles.summary: The report analyzes assets and liabilities totaling about ¥2.447 billion and describes rapid growth in fixed assets, loans to Manchukuo State Railways, debentures, and reserves. Railway, harbor, mining, and oil operations remained profitable, but investments in strategically motivated state lines created uncertainty for shareholders. Turner stresses that the Kwantung Army imposed costly military and industrial-development obligations while the Japanese government was reluctant to provide additional capital. He also discusses proposals for recapitalization and possible investment in kind by the Manchukuo government.

subfiles.title: Appendix to Despatch No. 124: South Manchuria Railway Company financial schedules
subfiles.from: South Manchuria Railway Company; compiled by the American Consulate at Dairen
subfiles.about: The appendix provides detailed balance-sheet, operating, development, debenture, share-price, and shareholder tables for fiscal 1938–39.
subfiles.summary: The schedules list assets and liabilities, the profit-and-loss account, disposition of profits, and revenue and expenditure by enterprise. Further tables trace changes in fixed assets and describe railway, harbor, mine, oil, coal-liquefaction, foundry, and housing projects. The appendix also lists outstanding debenture series, monthly share quotations, and principal private holders of South Manchuria Railway stock.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on locomotive parts held at Hong Kong
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum considers whether stranded locomotive parts should be brought to the attention of Chinese authorities as well as Japanese authorities.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews Peiping Despatch No. 2226 and recognizes that the Embassy had acted for American President Lines in approaching the Japanese Embassy. Because the shipment was consigned through the Bank of China to the Peiping–Suiyuan Railway, it concludes that the Chinese government at Chungking also had an apparent interest. It records the preparation of a telegram to Hong Kong recommending an approach to the Chinese authorities.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2226: Locomotive Parts Consigned to Peiping–Suiyuan Railway
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, United States Embassy at Peiping
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards correspondence about an undelivered shipment of locomotive parts and its approach to the Japanese Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart transmits W. F. Arndt’s letter concerning locomotive parts held by American President Lines at Hong Kong. He reports that the matter was presented to the Japanese Embassy in a memorandum dated August 18. Copies of Arndt’s letter, the memorandum, and the Embassy’s reply are enclosed.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning undelivered cargo from the SS President Monroe
subfiles.from: W. F. Arndt, American President Lines, Hong Kong
subfiles.about: Arndt requests Embassy assistance in obtaining a response about locomotive parts held at Hong Kong.
subfiles.summary: American President Lines had received no reply to its June 5 letter to the South Manchuria Railway’s North China Bureau. Storage charges on the cargo had risen to about $600, and delivery required presentation of the original bill of lading. Arndt asks the Embassy to seek the Japanese Embassy’s cooperation in securing a response from the proper authority.

subfiles.title: Letter to the North China Bureau concerning locomotive parts
subfiles.from: W. F. Arndt, American President Lines, Hong Kong
subfiles.to: North China Bureau, South Manchuria Railway, Tientsin
subfiles.about: Arndt asks the bureau to locate the original bill of lading or give instructions for disposing of locomotive parts awaiting delivery.
subfiles.summary: The letter identifies one case, 298 pieces, and 35 bundles of locomotive parts unloaded from the SS President Monroe on October 22, 1937. The shipment was covered by New York–Hong Kong bill of lading 6134 and consigned to the order of the Bank of China with notice to the Peiping–Suiyuan Railway. Because the consignee had not claimed it, Arndt sought immediate delivery instructions.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to the Japanese Embassy concerning the locomotive-parts shipment
subfiles.about: The memorandum requests Japanese assistance in obtaining a reply concerning the shipment held at Hong Kong.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy encloses Arndt’s June 5 letter to the South Manchuria Railway’s North China Bureau. It notes that no response had been received and that storage charges had reached approximately $600. The Japanese Embassy is asked to transmit the matter to the appropriate authorities and suggest that they reply to American President Lines.

subfiles.title: Copy of June 5 letter enclosed with the memorandum to the Japanese Embassy
subfiles.from: W. F. Arndt, American President Lines, Hong Kong
subfiles.to: North China Bureau, South Manchuria Railway, Tientsin
subfiles.about: This enclosure repeats the request to identify the holder of the bill of lading and arrange delivery of the locomotive parts.
subfiles.summary: The copied letter describes locomotive parts landed from the SS President Monroe in October 1937 and consigned through the Bank of China to the Peiping–Suiyuan Railway. It states that repeated arrival notices produced no claim for delivery. The bureau is asked to check whether it holds the original bill of lading and either claim the cargo or provide disposal instructions.

subfiles.title: Embassy reply to W. F. Arndt
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, United States Embassy at Peiping
subfiles.to: W. F. Arndt, American President Lines, Hong Kong
subfiles.about: The Embassy informs Arndt that it has referred his enclosure to the Japanese Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart acknowledges Arndt’s August 4 letter and its enclosure regarding the undelivered locomotive parts. He states that a copy was given to the Japanese Embassy at Peiping with a request that the matter be sent to the appropriate authorities for reply.

subfiles.title: Department telegram concerning Chinese interests in the locomotive parts
subfiles.to: United States Embassy, Peiping; repeated to Chungking
subfiles.about: The Department asks why Japanese authorities were approached and recommends notifying the Chinese government through American President Lines.
subfiles.summary: The Department observes that the goods were ordered while the Peiping–Suiyuan Railway remained under Chinese control and therefore appeared to concern the Chinese government directly. It asks the Embassy to explain its reasoning in referring the case to Japanese authorities. Unless circumstances dictated otherwise, the Embassy was to ask Hong Kong to advise American President Lines to approach the appropriate Chinese authorities without mentioning the prior Japanese approach.

subfiles.title: Peiping Embassy telegram explaining its approach to the Japanese Embassy
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, United States Embassy at Peiping
subfiles.about: The Embassy explains that it acted for American organizations and believed delivery through the Bank of China had already been attempted.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart states that the informal approach to the Japanese Embassy was made at the request of American President Lines and apparently with the approval of the Chinese Engineering and Development Company. The Embassy had asked only that the appropriate authority reply concerning the location of the original bill of lading. It assumed that American President Lines had already made an unsuccessful inquiry at the Bank of China’s Hong Kong office but offered to confirm this before further instructions were issued.

subfiles.title: Department telegram directing an approach to the Chinese authorities
subfiles.to: United States Embassy, Peiping; repeated to Chungking
subfiles.about: The Department reiterates that affirmative action should bring the stranded shipment to the Chinese government’s attention.
subfiles.summary: The Department reasons that the goods were purchased for the Peiping–Suiyuan Railway when it was under Chinese control, although its Peiping office was no longer controlled by the Chinese government. It therefore directs the Embassy to follow the procedure proposed in the October 10 telegram and arrange for the appropriate Chinese authorities to be notified.

subfiles.title: Peiping instruction to Hong Kong concerning American President Lines
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, United States Embassy at Peiping
subfiles.to: United States Consulate General, Hong Kong; reported to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The telegram directs Hong Kong to advise American President Lines to notify Chinese authorities while omitting mention of the Japanese approach.
subfiles.summary: Hong Kong is instructed to tell W. F. Arndt that American President Lines should bring its inability to deliver the materials to the attention of the appropriate Chinese government authorities. The shipping company is also to be discreetly advised not to mention that the case had already been raised with Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: Hong Kong confirmation of action on the locomotive-parts case
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; sent to Peiping and repeated to Chungking
subfiles.about: Southard confirms that the Department’s requested advice was conveyed to American President Lines.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports that the representative of American President Lines was informed on October 20 as instructed. It closes the section’s correspondence by confirming execution of the referral to Chinese authorities.
